system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2176-04-08 08:33:00 to 2176-04-08 21:40:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A male patient with end-stage renal disease and a history of heart failure was admitted with acute shortness of breath after returning from church. He reported sudden onset of dyspnea, dry cough, leg swelling, and recent weight gain. In the ED, his oxygen saturation was in the mid-80s, requiring BiPAP support. Initial labs revealed severe hyperkalemia (K+ 8.2) and elevated BUN/creatinine, prompting emergent hemodialysis, which corrected his potassium and improved his respiratory status. He later developed chest pain with EKG changes and elevated troponins, consistent with a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction. A nuclear stress test showed normal myocardial perfusion and preserved ejection fraction, so he was managed medically without intervention. His pulmonary edema improved with dialysis and supportive care. He was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to monitor weight, continue home medications, and follow up with cardiology and nephrology.

Subendocardial infarction, initial episode of care

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ man with history of end-stage renal disease on
hemodialysis, status post transplant with rejection with coronary artery
disease, who presents with abdominal pain during hemodialysis.  Rule out
mesenteric ischemia.

COMPARISON:  CT of the abdomen and pelvis from ___.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT images were acquired through the abdomen and pelvis with and
without IV contrast.  The ED physician ___ that the
patient was due for dialysis today.  Multiplanar reformations were obtained
and reviewed.

The partially imaged lungs are clear.  The partially imaged heart is
unremarkable.

CT OF THE ABDOMEN WITH IV CONTRAST:  The liver, spleen, both adrenals,
pancreas and gallbladder are unremarkable.  Both native kidneys are atrophic
with multiple unchanged, hypodense cysts within them.  There is a large right
inferior pole parapelvic cyst.  No abdominal, retroperitoneal or mesenteric
lymphadenopathy by CT size criteria is present.  No abdominal free fluid or
free air is present.  There is mild diffuse calcific atherosclerosis of the
abdominal vasculature with significant calcific atherosclerosis at the origin
and proximal portion of the superior mesenteric artery.  The small and large
bowel loops are unremarkable.  The appendix is normal as well.  No abdominal
free fluid or free air is present.  Note is made of two duodenal diverticulum
in the ___ and ___ part of the duodenum.

CT OF THE PELVIS WITH IV CONTRAST:  A right transplanted pelvic kidney is
small, atrophic but unchanged compared to the previous examination.  The
rectum, sigmoid colon, prostate and seminal vesicles are unremarkable.  A
small amount of fat is noted within the wall of the collapsed bladder,
unchanged, which can be a normal finding.  No pelvic or inguinal
lymphadenopathy or pelvic free fluid is present.

OSSEOUS STRUCTURES:  The visible osseous structures show no suspicious lytic
or blastic lesions or fractures.  There is mild anterior osteophyte formation
of the lower lumbar spine.

IMPRESSION:  Severe calcification and narrowing in the proximal and at the
origin of the SMA.  No evidence of mesenteric ischemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you had some abdominal pain during dialysis this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, right around my belly button. It came on suddenly while I was in the dialysis chair. I’ve never felt anything like it before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Was the pain sharp or crampy? Did it go anywhere else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It was crampy at first, then got sharper. It stayed in the middle, but I did feel some chest tightness afterward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s important. Given your history of heart disease and recent heart attack, we had to check if this was cardiac. Your EKG and troponins were stable, so we think the chest pain is likely related to the abdominal issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s a relief. But what’s causing the belly pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We ordered a CT scan to check for a serious condition called mesenteric ischemia—where blood flow to the intestines is reduced.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that what I have?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The good news is, there’s no sign of ischemia or blockage in the intestines. But the scan did show severe calcification and narrowing at the start of the artery that supplies blood to your intestines—the superior mesenteric artery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s narrowed, but not blocked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That narrowing could still reduce blood flow, especially during times of stress—like dialysis—when your body redirects blood. That might explain the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Since there’s no acute blockage, we’ll manage this conservatively. You’ll have dialysis today as scheduled, and we’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You just finished hemodialysis, and I’m glad to hear the abdominal pain didn’t return during the session.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s been much better. I only had a little discomfort at the start, but it faded quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. We’ll keep managing your vascular risk factors—blood pressure, cholesterol, and diabetes control—to prevent further narrowing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re going to discharge you now. Continue your regular medications, watch for any return of belly or chest pain, and follow up with your nephrologist and cardiologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ll be more careful during dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. And if the pain comes back, don’t wait—seek care right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve learned my lesson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, keep monitoring your blood pressure and weight, and stay on your statin and antiplatelet meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been consistent with those. Any dietary changes I should make?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stick to your renal diet—low sodium, low potassium—and avoid heavy meals that might stress your gut. Small, frequent meals may help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ll see you in follow-up, but call sooner if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. You’re cleared to go home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. Have a good day.

summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with end-stage renal disease, status post kidney transplant with complications, and a history of coronary artery disease and recent subendocardial infarction, was admitted for acute periumbilical abdominal pain that occurred during hemodialysis. Concern for mesenteric ischemia prompted a CT angiogram, which revealed severe calcific atherosclerosis and narrowing of the superior mesenteric artery but no evidence of acute ischemia. His symptoms improved without intervention, and he completed a session of hemodialysis without recurrence of pain. The chest pain reported was evaluated and deemed non-acute. He was discharged in stable condition with instructions to continue medical management of vascular risk factors, adhere to his renal diet, and follow up with nephrology and cardiology.
